headlines.summary: After elected officials voiced outrage over Google turning off search at schools that ban AI, the company said search can be turned back on with AI Overviews.
headlines.article_text: Google responds to outrage over removing search in schools that ban AI Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Politicians including Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani criticized Google following reports that the company would restrict search at schools that ban AI. Google responded to the outrage, saying that Gemini, Gemini Notebook and search will be turned off by default, and schools can choose to turn one or all of them back on. Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told the New York Times that "Search and AI are deeply integrated." In this article META Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT David Tramontan | SOPA Images | Lightrocket | Getty Images Google is playing defense on Tuesday after a political backlash to its new policy surrounding use of artificial intelligence in schools. In a blog post titled "Designing responsible AI for learning," Google said it's bringing AI into its Classroom offering with a product called Guided Learning. The New York Times published a story saying that the company will turn off search for schools that reject AI entirely. Following the Times' story, prominent left-leaning politicians, including Sen. Bernie Sanders from Vermont and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani voiced their outrage on social media. "Google is trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools," Mamdani wrote on X. Sanders wrote that "Google is threatening schools," referring to the policy as "extortion." Google responded later in the day. In a post on X , the company said its new policy was meant to give schools more choice over how students interact with AI. Google said its Gemini chatbot, Gemini Notebook and search are turned off by default, and that "schools are in control," with the ability to turn them as they see fit. "We are also updating Search for schools to make it better for learning," Google wrote. "Specifically, AI Mode and AI Overviews will offer step-by-step guided learning through problems, so that students don't get quick answers to schoolwork." The company's post didn't explicitly respond to the claim that access to search requires use of AI. However, Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told the Times that "Search and AI are deeply integrated." A Google spokesperson referred CNBC to the X post when asked for comment. Google's broader practices have come under fire in recent years, with the company losing antitrust cases over its search and advertising businesses. Former Federal Trade Commission Chair Lina Khan aggressively pursued Google and other tech giants, including Meta and Amazon . Khan said in a post on X on Tuesday that Google's new AI for learning policy highlights "the danger of allowing an unregulated monopolist to control an essential service." It's the latest controversy related to the impact of technology on children and the role leading internet companies are playing in delivering information. In August, Meta reached a landmark $16.7 billion settlement in its child safety trial after a number of state attorneys general accused the company of misrepresenting the extent of child mental health harms caused by apps like Facebook and Instagram . The same month, OpenAI launched ChatGPT for Teens after state attorneys general launched an investigation into the company's safety practices, with Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, a Republican, filing a lawsuit in June. The nonprofit Common Sense Media recently gave Google's AI overviews an " unacceptable risk " rating. Last month, Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., and Josh Hawley, R-Mo., launched an inquiry over Google's push of AI into classrooms. Google introduced AI overviews as a search function in May 2024 . — CNBC's MacKenzie Sigalos contributed to this report. WATCH: Meta settled its child safety lawsuit. headlines.article_text: CrowdStrike's new kill switch can stop rogue AI agents in their tracks, CEO says Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz said the company's new technology allows businesses to stop rogue AI agents, prevent them from restarting and cut off their network access. Kurtz says he sees AI agent safety as a major growth opportunity for CrowdStrike, pointing to growing enterprise demand and an expanded partnership with Anthropic. In this article CRWD Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 2:10 02:10 CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz talks new 'AI kill switch' Mad Money with Jim Cramer CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz said Tuesday that the cybersecurity company can now shut down rogue artificial intelligence agents. CrowdStrike's new kill switch , announced Tuesday at its Fal.Con Europe conference, allows security teams to terminate misbehaving agents, prevent them from restarting and cut off their network access. It is designed to give humans more power over artificial intelligence models and systems, as concerns about how to control agents grow. "Everyone is building AI agents, but they never had the off button, and now they do," Kurtz told CNBC's Jim Cramer on " Mad Money ." "It's going to be an incredibly important part of making sure that AI agents run and operate safely." The AI Kill Switch, as CrowdStrike calls it, is part of the company's Falcon Guardian platform, which monitors AI agents operating within an organization. The technology, which is available immediately, is aimed at addressing AI safety concerns surrounding the rapid adoption of AI agents. In September, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for slowing AI development over safety concerns, a position backed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman . Kurtz argued at the time that slowing AI development would not eliminate existing security risks, which he said underscored the need for safeguards as companies deploy autonomous systems. Kurtz said Tuesday that CrowdStrike's new kill switch represents a significant shift in cybersecurity, which has traditionally focused on protecting companies from external threats. As businesses rely more on AI agents, he argued that security providers must also ensure those systems operate safely within their own organizations. "Enabling agents to work safely is a massive market opportunity for CrowdStrike," Kurtz said. "We have AI capabilities to prevent these breaches from happening on the outside, and we also have the capabilities to make sure that agents are basically doing what they are instructed to do." The CEO compared the technology to airbags in cars, arguing that safeguards are necessary even when AI systems are designed to operate correctly. "If they go outside of those guardrails at runtime, we can kill those agents," he said. CrowdStrike is seeing growing demand for its security tools as businesses adopt AI. Kurtz pointed to CrowdStrike's partnership with Anthropic to protect its Claude Cowork product: He said enterprise customers had pushed for CrowdStrike's technology to be integrated before they deployed Anthropic's offerings. "Our customers went to Anthropic and said, 'We need CrowdStrike before we can deploy AI,'" Kurtz said. "I think it says volumes that customers would not roll out AI without CrowdStrike." headlines.article_text: Stocks making the biggest moves after hours: ANET, AMD, SMCI, SWKS Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Here are some of the companies making headlines in extended trading. CVS Health — Shares were slightly higher after The Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that CVS would split off its retail pharmacy business . The company will divide into two publicly traded companies, with the breakup expected in the first half of 2028, the Journal reported. Duolingo — The language learning software company surged 11% after reporting third-quarter revenue of $309 million. That topped an LSEG consensus of $303 million. Monthly active users totaled 153 million for the quarter, exceeding a 149 million forecast. Adjusted EBITDA margin also topped expectations. Alight — The employee benefits consultancy popped 17% after raising its outlook for the full-year 2026. Alight sees revenue in a range of $2.115 billion to $2.125 billion, versus the FactSet consensus estimate of $2.09 billion. Adjusted EBITDA guidance of $410 million to $420 million also beat the Street's estimates of $404.4 million. Avis Budget Group — The car rental agency tumbled more than 7% on mixed third-quarter results. Avis earned $5.15 a share, a steep decline from $10.11 per share in the year-earlier period. Revenue clocked in at $3.44 billion, slightly ahead of a FactSet consensus of $3.42 billion. Advanced Micro Devices — The chipmaker jumped 7% after reporting stronger-than-expected third-quarter earnings . Adjusted earnings of $2.09 per share topped estimates for $1.95, according to analysts polled by LSEG. Revenue forecasts for the current quarter also came in above estimates. Toast — The restaurant management software company slipped 4% despite delivering third-quarter financials quarter that topped estimates, according to FactSet. Toast also said CFO Elena Gomez will leave the company at the end of 2026 and will be replaced by senior vice president of finance Michael Senno. Skyworks Solutions — The provider of wireless networking services slumped about 16% after guidance for the current quarter disappointed the Street. Skyworks anticipates adjusted earnings of about $1.25 per share and revenue of $1.80 billion to $1.90 billion in the fiscal first quarter, short of LSEG consensus estimates of $1.50 a share and $1.99 billion. Skyworks completed its combination with Qorvo in early October, and the first quarter marks the first combined quarter for the two. Super Micro Computer — Shares of the server company jumped more than 9% after Super Micro earnings per share and revenue beat Wall Street estimates. For fiscal year 2027, the company expects net sales to range between $72 billion and $82 billion, above the LSEG consensus for $69.17 billion. Arista Networks — The cloud networking company gained 12% after current-quarter guidance topped estimates. Arista sees fourth-quarter earnings of $1.26 to $1.30 per share on revenue of $3.9 billion to $4.0 billion. Analysts surveyed by LSEG were looking for $1.15 per share and $3.60 billion. Block — The fintech stock rallied more than 6% after Block posted third-quarter earnings and revenue that exceeded expectations, and raised guidance for the full year ending December. Adjusted earnings of $1.13 per share topped the $1.03 LSEG consensus estimate, while revenue of $6.72 billion beat the $6.59 billion consensus. Freshworks — The software stock tumbled about 6% even after the customer support ticketing company posted stronger-than-expected third-quarter results and full-year guidance. Freshworks earned an adjusted 22 cents per share on revenue of $245.4 million in the latest quarter, above earnings of 18 cents on revenue of $245.1 million analysts polled by FactSet were anticipating. The stock has recently outperformed, rallying more than 20% over the past three months. — CNBC's Sarah Min, Davis Giangiulio, Ananya Chetia and Fred Imbert contributed reporting.

headlines.summary: AMD reported better-than-expected third-quarter results, driven by booming sales of AI chips
headlines.article_text: AMD (AMD) Q3 earnings report 2026 Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points AMD reported third-quarter earnings that beat Wall Street expectations, with revenue jumping 45% from a year earlier. Revenue in the chipmaker's data center business nearly doubled, and CEO Lisa Su said AMD can meet accelerating demand for AI chips. The stock is up 129% so far this year, but sold off in recent days on industrywide fears of overspending on AI infrastructure. In this article AMD Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Lisa Su, chair and chief executive officer of Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (AMD), speaks during the company's Gamers Day event in Seoul, South Korea, on Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026. SeongJoon Cho | Bloomberg | Getty Images Advanced Micro Devices reported third-quarter earnings on Tuesday that beat Wall Street's expectations, with revenue jumping 45% and data center sales nearly doubling from a year earlier. The stock was up 8% in extended trading. Here's how the chipmaker did versus LSEG consensus estimates for the quarter: Earnings per share : $2.09 adjusted vs. $1.95 expected Revenue : $13.38 billion vs. $13.09 billion expected Revenue increased from $9.25 billion a year earlier, AMD said in a statement . Neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius rallied earlier Tuesday and remained higher after AMD reported results. CEO Lisa Su said on the earnings call that she expects server revenue to double year over year in 2027 and data center AI growth to accelerate even faster than the company had projected 90 days ago. The company expects data center to drive the majority of its revenue and earnings growth. "We have worked across our supply chain to secure the wafers, substrates, advanced packaging, memory, and other key components needed to support much higher growth next year," Su said on the earnings call. AMD's report comes days after Intel disclosed similar data center growth, with revenue in that segment up 78% in the third quarter. But Intel's stock plummeted 29% on Friday over concerns about weak guidance and Intel's ability to meet demand . The data center unit makes up the majority of AMD's business, accounting for 64% of overall revenue, up from 47% a year ago. After years spent chasing Nvidia in the market for artificial intelligence graphics processing units, or GPUs, AMD's central processing units, or CPUs, are experiencing a major resurgence with the rise of agentic AI apps like Meta 's Muse. AMD's server CPUs are key for agentic apps because they power virtual machines and can run for hours on their own. Demand from agentic AI boosted AMD shares to a record in October. "Adoption is just starting, and we expect demand to grow sharply as agents are deployed more broadly and take on more complex work," Su said on the earnings call with analysts. PC market struggles AMD's stock is up about 125% this year, but it saw three consecutive days of losses before rallying on Tuesday amid an industrywide sell-off tied to fears about overspending on AI. AMD is also a major player in the weakening PC market, which Intel blamed for its poor outlook last week. AMD and Intel are the largest makers of traditional x86 processors that power many laptops and desktops, while other laptops rely on Arm -based processors from the likes of Qualcomm and Apple. Global PC shipments declined 4% in the second quarter from a year earlier due to soaring costs for memory and other components, according to Counterpoint Research . AMD reports PC chip sales in a segment combined with gaming chips. Revenue in that business fell 8% from a year earlier to $3.7 billion. Gaming revenue was down 40% from a year ago. For the fourth quarter, AMD said it expects about $17 billion in revenue, beating the $16.2 billion average analyst estimate, according to LSEG. AMD sees its gross margin for the quarter coming in at 55%, slightly below the average estimate of 55.3%, according to StreetAccount. AMD also sells data center GPUs and full rack-scale systems called Helios that compete directly with Nvidia's Grace Blackwell and Vera Rubin systems. Meta, Microsoft , Anthropic, OpenAI, and Oracle are all beginning to use AMD Helios in their data centers. Meta said last week that its Helios racks are up and running, and AMD agreed to invest $1 billion in Meta's equity offering. AMD has also committed to investing up to $5 billion in Anthropic, which unveiled its highly anticipated prospectus last week as it inches closer to a potentially historic initial public offering . During a visit to Taiwan in October, Su said she plans to "substantially increase our supply in 2027." Su and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang have both made multiple trips to Taiwan and South Korea this year, holding meetings with key suppliers like Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company and memory leaders SK Hynix and Samsung. In September, AMD said it would acquire World Labs for $8.2 billion in an all-stock deal. The San Francisco-based AI lab, founded by industry pioneer Fei-Fei Li, is developing a so-called world model that simulates 3D environments to aid in developing robots and other physically grounded AI applications.
